slides.say: Given: x and y are positive numbers, and x is bigger than y. Which of the following must be true?

Must be true means true for every allowed pair. So one allowed pair where a choice fails is enough to rule that choice out. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, plugging in numbers, and then with algebra, to see why the answer always works.
[short pause] Let's start with easy whole numbers that fit the givens. x is three and y is two. Both are positive, and three is bigger than two.
at: x is three and y is two

slides.say: Choice number one, x squared is bigger than x. Three squared is nine, and nine is bigger than three, so it works here. Choice number two, x y is bigger than y. Three times two is six, and six is bigger than two. It works. Choice number three, x squared is bigger than y squared. Nine is bigger than four. It works too.
Choice number four, x over y is bigger than x. Three over two is one and a half, and one and a half is not bigger than three. So choice number four fails for an allowed pair, and it's out.

Three choices still work, so one pair wasn't enough. Positive numbers can also be between zero and one, and there, squaring makes a number smaller. So let's try x is one half and y is one quarter. Both are positive, and one half is bigger than one quarter.
at: x is one half and y

slides.say: Choice number one. One half squared is one quarter, and one quarter is not bigger than one half, so it's out. Choice number two. One half times one quarter is one eighth, and one eighth is not bigger than one quarter, so it's out too.
at: One half squared is one quarter

slides.say: Only choice number three is left, so choice number three is our answer.
at: so choice number three is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now let's see why choice number three is true for every allowed pair. x squared minus y squared is, in brackets, x minus y, times, in brackets, x plus y.
at: x squared minus y squared is

slides.say: x is bigger than y, so x minus y is positive. Both numbers are positive, so x plus y is positive too. A positive number times a positive number is positive. So x squared minus y squared is positive, which means x squared is bigger than y squared, always. Choice number three. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: so x minus y is positive
